rv.q: Cyndi Lauper’s songs have stood the test of time.
I feel like a heel for saying it but this Kinky Boots is soulless.
It’s an enjoyable night out, and a brilliantly unlikely story, but in terms of the craft of musical theatre, Kinky Boots leans towards the pedestrian.
The result is a genuine treat – a sequin-soaked fantasia of mutual understanding and acceptance that sits very comfortably on the West End’s biggest stage.
Foster’s production is more workmanlike than inspired but Radebe’s star power, Cardle’s warm magnetism and Bowman’s comic joie de vivre keep it buoyantly watchable.
This production is a blaze of colour at a dismally grey time.
Still, it’s a welcome excuse to revisit a classic, sewn together just enough originality to make it feel like a stylish homage, not a cynical knock off.
Radebe and Cardle knock this Kinky Boots out of the park.
Joyous and uplifting, Kinky Boots is just the tonic in an increasingly divided and divisive world.
Radebe is effervescent and engaging in the lead although I struggled with his South African accent on a few occasions.
Niggles aside, however, for those wanting an uplifting evening of escapism with a message of love and self-acceptance, Kinky Boots more than delivers.
But neither book nor songs offer enough to buy a ticket to a show that leans lazily into the North in Northampton - complete with flat caps, vests and tats, and wayward accents.
